near_miss.lead: Dark night: myrkt / nótt and мрклој ноћи / мрака
near_miss.why_not: Norse has impersonal darkness at night; the Serbian examples address night or specify its darkness in lyric language. The Norse text does not reproduce the Serbian epithet or full-of-darkness figure. Searches of Menota XML and Vuk pages.jsonl found ordinary night-darkness expressions in further texts, including Finnboga saga and Vuk 13012, 1541, 7782. Search hits were manually screened because the loose patterns also retrieve unrelated words. Cognate darkness/night vocabulary is plausible, but such predictable description, with different constructions and late Serbian witnesses, does not establish an inherited phrase.

The Norse first passage compares treatment of one woman as daughter versus sister; the second identifies one woman by two relations. Birchbark 531 concerns two women, a sister and her daughter. The Irish genealogy likewise distributes relations among different persons. Cognate kinship words do not constitute a shared merism or formula here.

Norse faðir and móðir are subjects of urðu fegin after their daughter recovers. Sanskrit pitṛ-mātṛṣu is a locative complement describing filial conduct, while mātṛ-pitṛ-vat compares a creator with parents. The shared wert root has different predication and argument structure. The parental pair alone is ordinary kinship language.

near_miss.lead: Water sprinkling and drawing: ausa / vatn versus ἀφύσσω / ὕδωρ
near_miss.why_not: The Norse passages concern pouring/sprinkling water on a newborn in a naming rite, with instrumental dative vatni; Odyssey 10.56 concerns replenishing water ashore, with accusative object ὕδωρ. Searching the Homer treebank found the drawing-water construction also at Odyssey 4.358-359 and 9.85-86, with ὕδωρ tagged OBJ. This confirms a Greek collocation but supplies no naming rite or congruent cross-branch syntax. Iliad 11.462 is shouting, not drawing water; its retrieval rests on a faulty mapping.

Þorsteinn, not the sun, is subject of stóð upp; við sól sets the time of his rising. In RV 4.1.17c sūryaḥ is the subject of tiṣṭhat. The high place borg versus br̥hataḥ likewise does not share a syntactic function. The three apparent cognate correspondences do not form the same phrase.

Irish co siair a máthar contains siair, dative singular of siur after co, plus genitive singular máthar. Norse systur Beru móður Egils means sister of Bera, mother of Egill: móður is in apposition to Beru, not a genitive depending directly on systur. Both identify a maternal aunt, but the relationship naturally explains the shared kinship vocabulary. The two Irish passages are versions of the same text, not independent branches; their additional automatic mappings include errors.

near_miss.lead: Snow falling versus Umbrian holtu ninctu
near_miss.why_not: Norse has literal snow as subject of fell in a travel impediment. Umbrian has a sequence of ritual imperatives against enemies, not snow as subject of falling. Even accepting the supplied etymologies, the syntax and contexts do not match. A text search for ninctu in the local Ik u vina UD test file (umbrian-ud-ikuvina/xum_ikuvina-ud-test.conllu) returned no occurrence and provided no additional support; no correction of its debated interpretation is asserted here.

near_miss.lead: Eyes and nostrils as a body-part pair
near_miss.why_not: Egil vomits into a man’s eyes and nostrils (and mouth in the following context); Lucretius lists sensory organs in an argument about sensation, with different order and additional members. The Russian line is visibly damaged by OCR and cannot securely establish a matching construction. Natural adjacency of facial organs is insufficient for a distinctive inherited merism.

The Norse clauses place an announcement in spring and a projected voyage in summer. The Atharvavedic passages enumerate seasons as protective powers. These are separate temporal adjuncts versus coordinated ritual season lists, not a shared two-member formula.

near_miss.lead: Father/mother and the rejection of killing parents (Greek and Vedic partners)
near_miss.why_not: Herodotus reports a Persian assertion that a true child has never killed his own parents; the Vedic passage prays that a child born under a dangerous constellation not injure father or mother. The parental objects are cognate, but the killing verbs are not matched, and negative report versus apotropaic wish differs. The widespread kinship taboo is not distinctive enough to demonstrate common inherited wording. Norse is a genealogy; Homer describes Achilles’ parentage; Lucretius describes plague deaths. Those anchors do not strengthen the specific equation.

The Norse sailing expression byr gaf was checked against the Greek partner’s mappings. Greek φορέουσι describes snakes bearing horns, and πεφυκότα their grown horns; there is no wind or navigation context. Shared roots behind byrr and φορέω, and búnir and πεφυκότα, do not create shared phraseology.

Norse Lǫgðusk ... sváfu ... nóttina and Russian Легъ ... спать ... ночь share ordinary sleep vocabulary with three inherited roots. Norse coordinates finite predicates; Russian has a purpose infinitive. Menota searches found further ordinary lying/sleeping sequences in Laxdaela and Njals saga, and the Rybnikov volume has multiple lie/sleep combinations with varying time/place modifiers (including text lines 4843, 5433, 7910, 10353). These establish within-tradition recurrence but no distinctive inherited figure or cross-branch formula; the late byliny witnesses make inheritance still harder to establish.

The Norse instruction combines offering one’s own head to a king with grasping the king’s foot, a supplication gesture involving different possessors. Lucretius lists head, feet, and hands as possible bodily locations. This is not the same head-to-foot merism; the other partners concern plants or infantry.

Norse egg is the noun edge in an inspection of a damaged axe; Homer ὀξέσι is an adjective modifying weapons used in close combat. Even if the supplied axe equation is accepted, axe/edge and sharp/axe are predictable tool descriptions, with no distinctive shared context or construction. The supplied second mapping of egg as an egg laid by a bird is inapplicable.
